extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians of mathematics, and educated readers interested in critiques of mathematical and scientific claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for evaluating mathematical, scientific, and related polemical writings—especially fringe/paradoxical claims—covering evidence, clarity, publication, logical usage, and plausibility. Emphasis is on how to judge authorship, novelty, readability, and the soundness of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and plain style in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing (legal, scientific, or popular) should be clear and understandable; obscure learned words and unnecessarily abstruse diction impede comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan illustrates this with the anecdote that Acts of Parliament—'written in the clearest and plainest style in which anything can be written'—are nonetheless often unintelligible to most readers, and attributes much obscurity to un-boiled (i.e., untranslated/specialized) Greek words introduced by learned sources (the 'council of Nice' metaphor). The practical guidance is to avoid hard or imported technical vocabulary without explanation; plain exposition increases intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous documentary evidence for extraordinary biographical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary claims about early prodigies (age, achievements) require contemporary certification, public proofs, or other documentary attestations to be credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clairaut's youthful authorship is accepted because his age was publicly certified and he gave public proofs at twelve; such contemporary attestations 'remove all doubt.' For claims of precocity, prefer birth records, dated publications, contemporaneous testimonials, or public demonstrations as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and priority require independent circulation or naming evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of authorship or priority are supported when works or theorems circulate under an author's name or when contemporaries reference them by that name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan uses Pascal's hexagram circulating under his name by age nineteen as evidence supporting early authorship. Bibliographic or anecdotal claims should be corroborated by independent circulation, citations, or named circulation rather than by later tradition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify extraordinary claims against primary sources/editions
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone asserts a revision or retraction (or any significant textual/editional claim), check the primary editions or authoritative sources rather than relying on hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the claim that Newton retracted his theories before death: De Morgan points out there is 'no retraction in the third edition of the Principia' and thus recommends checking the actual editions. Always consult original publications/editions to confirm asserted textual facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish serious speculation from fiction and demand rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative scientific or mathematical proposals should be judged by standards of rigour and evidence; mere imaginative or rhetorical treatment (fiction) does not have the same obligation to empirical or logical substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan notes how close 'pure speculation comes to fable' and contrasts 'good fiction' (sublime) with 'bad speculation' (ridiculous). When assessing claims, determine whether the author presents a serious methodological case or is offering literary/fanciful conjecture, and apply appropriate standards of proof accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic titles alone are insufficient to determine authorship or content
rubrics_metrics.description: A title or catalogue entry does not by itself resolve questions of authorship, priority, or the actual content of a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regarding Bradwardine and the quadrature tract, De Morgan warns 'The titles do not make it quite sure that Bradwardine is the quadrator; it may be Peter Sanchez after all.' Always seek internal evidence, prefaces, colophons, printers' notes, and other bibliographic details before attributing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility checks on publishing claims and bibliographic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary bibliographic or publication claims (e.g., improbable volume counts, odd subscription lists) should be checked for typographical or factual error and for plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan questions an entry promising '8 volumes' on the theory of parallels and treats the claim sceptically. Verify whether misprints or exaggerations are present (e.g., 'eight volumes' could be a misprint) and cross-check with library records, catalogues, or publisher data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims to what the argument actually supports; avoid overclaiming consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a paradox or observation is interesting ('a fair one'), authors should not draw outlandish or broad consequences without rigorous derivation; scope of inference must match the strength of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan accepts that Wood's paradox about velocities is 'deserving of investigation' but doubts the easy derivation of tides, trade-winds, etc. Evaluate whether claimed consequences follow logically and quantitatively from the premises before accepting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability, punctuation, and typography affect accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation—punctuation, capitalization, and typographic conventions—matters for readability; extreme departures (e.g., no stops except at paragraph ends) hinder comprehension and usability of mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The case of Dobson's Elements of Geometry (virtually unpunctuated and prolix) shows that lack of conventional punctuation and concise organization renders a work nearly unreadable. Authors and publishers should maintain readable typography and organizational clarity; reviewers should note such defects as serious impediments to communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical and technical terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Misuse or confusion of logical vocabulary (e.g., 'cumulative' vs 'distributive') indicates sloppy reasoning and can mislead readers; technical terms should be used in their correct sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan criticizes an author for calling distinct evidential structures 'cumulative' when they are 'distributive.' Ensure terminology aligns with standard logical meanings; when introducing novel usage, define terms explicitly to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogies must respect conceptual distinctions (avoid category errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical reasoning is acceptable only when the items compared are of comparable categorical status; conflating properties with persons or attributes with entities leads to bad physics/theology or invalid argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan rejects the sun/light/heat analogy as bad physics and worse theology because it treats properties as if they were persons. Check that analogies preserve relevant structure and do not collapse essential differences between the compared items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing conspiratorial motives without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that scientific doctrines are upheld because of conspiracies, patronage, or partisan rewards should be treated with scepticism and require concrete evidence rather than conjecture about motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Richard Phillips's assertions about pensions and a plot to reward Newtonian partisans are presented as an example of corrosive suspicion. Critiques should focus on arguments and evidence rather than unproven allegations about motives or cabals.
